But hasn't the worthy one's hatred been abandoned… delusion been abandoned… conceit been abandoned… wrong view been abandoned… doubt been abandoned… sluggishness been abandoned… restlessness been abandoned… shamelessness been abandoned… lack of moral fear been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to arise in the future? Yes. If the worthy one's lack of moral fear has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, so that it is no longer subject to arise in the future, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. But hasn't the worthy one developed the path for the abandoning of greed? Yes. If the worthy one has developed the path for the abandoning of greed, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. But hasn't the worthy one developed the foundations of mindfulness for the abandoning of greed… developed the right strivings… developed the bases of psychic power… developed the faculties… developed the powers… developed the factors of awakening? Yes. If the worthy one has developed the factors of awakening for the abandoning of greed, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. But hasn't the worthy one developed the path for the abandoning of hatred… for the abandoning of lack of moral fear… developed the factors of awakening? Yes. If the worthy one has developed the factors of awakening for the abandoning of lack of moral fear, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship." ^5-260

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. But isn't the worthy one free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, one who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the load, who has reached their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, who is completely liberated through final knowledge, who has lifted the cross-bar, filled in the moat, pulled out the pillar, who has no bolt, a noble one, whose banner is lowered, whose burden is put down, who is unfettered, who has won complete victory; by whom suffering has been fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realized, the path developed; by whom what is to be directly known has been directly known, what is to be fully understood has been fully understood, what is to be abandoned has been abandoned, what is to be developed has been developed, what is to be realized has been realized? Yes. If the worthy one is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion… and what is to be realized has been realized, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship." ^5-261

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? ( ) [(Yes.) (Ka.)] A temporarily liberated worthy one falls away from arahantship; a worthy one who is not temporarily liberated does not fall away from arahantship. Does a temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Does a worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship [variant: na parihāyatīti (Ka.)]? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. Does a temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
Greed has been abandoned by the temporarily liberated worthy one — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Greed has been abandoned by the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
Hatred has been abandoned by the temporarily liberated worthy one… lack of moral fear has been abandoned — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Lack of moral fear has been abandoned by the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The temporarily liberated worthy one has developed the path for the abandoning of greed — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated has developed the path for the abandoning of greed — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The temporarily liberated worthy one has developed the foundations of mindfulness for the abandoning of greed… developed the right strivings… developed the bases of psychic power… developed the faculties… developed the powers… developed the factors of awakening — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated has developed the foundations of mindfulness for the abandoning of greed… developed the factors of awakening — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The temporarily liberated worthy one has developed the path for the abandoning of hatred… for the abandoning of lack of moral fear… developed the factors of awakening — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated has developed the path for the abandoning of lack of moral fear… developed the factors of awakening — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said…
The temporarily liberated worthy one is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, one who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the load, who has reached their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, who is completely liberated through final knowledge, who has lifted the cross-bar, filled in the moat, pulled out the pillar, who has no bolt, a noble one, whose banner is lowered, whose burden is put down, who is unfettered, who has won complete victory; by whom suffering has been fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realized, the path developed; by whom what is to be directly known has been directly known, what is to be fully understood has been fully understood, what is to be abandoned has been abandoned, what is to be developed has been developed, what is to be realized has been realized — does the temporarily liberated worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion… and what is to be realized has been realized — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated fall away from arahantship? That should not be said. ^5-262

Greed has been abandoned by the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. Greed has been abandoned by the temporarily liberated worthy one — does the temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
Hatred has been abandoned by the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated… lack of moral fear has been abandoned — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. Lack of moral fear has been abandoned by the temporarily liberated worthy one — does the temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated has developed the path for the abandoning of greed… developed the factors of awakening — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. The temporarily liberated worthy one has developed the path for the abandoning of greed… developed the factors of awakening — does the temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated has developed the path for the abandoning of hatred… for the abandoning of lack of moral fear… developed the factors of awakening — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. The temporarily liberated worthy one has developed the path for the abandoning of lack of moral fear… developed the factors of awakening — does the temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
The worthy one who is not temporarily liberated is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion… and what is to be realized has been realized — does the worthy one who is not temporarily liberated not fall away from arahantship? Yes. The temporarily liberated worthy one is free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion… and what is to be realized has been realized — does the temporarily liberated worthy one not fall away from arahantship? That should not be said… ^5-263

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Did the elder Sāriputta fall away from arahantship? That should not be said. Did the elder Mahāmoggallāna [variant: mahāmoggalāno (Ka.)]… the elder Mahākassapa… the elder Mahākaccāyana [variant: mahākaccāno (M. Ni. 1.202 and elsewhere)]… the elder Mahākoṭṭhika [variant: mahākoṭṭhito (Sī., Syā., Kaṃ., Pī.)]… the elder Mahāpanthaka fall away from arahantship? That should not be said.
Did the elder Sāriputta not fall away from arahantship? Yes. If the elder Sāriputta did not fall away from arahantship, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Did the elder Mahāmoggallāna… the elder Mahākassapa… the elder Mahākaccāyana… the elder Mahākoṭṭhika… the elder Mahāpanthaka not fall away from arahantship? Yes. If the elder Mahāpanthaka did not fall away from arahantship, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Comparison with the noble persons. ^5-264

#### Falling Away: Proof from the Discourses ^5-2-3-0

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"High and low are the ways of practice [variant: paṭipādā (Aṭṭha.)] made known by the ascetic;
they do not go to the far shore twice, yet this is not to be thought of as reached only once" [Su. Ni. 719, in the Sutta Nipāta]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one falls away from arahantship."
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Is there anything still to be cut for one who has cut? That should not be said.
Is there anything still to be cut for one who has cut? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"One who is free from craving, without grasping, for whom there is nothing left to do —
for one who has cut, there is nothing still to be cut; the snare of the floods has been removed"?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "there is something still to be cut for one who has cut." ^5-265

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Is there any adding to what has been done? That should not be said.
Is there any adding to what has been done? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"For that monk, rightly liberated, whose mind is at peace,
there is no adding to what has been done, and nothing remains to be done.
"As a rock that is one solid mass is not shaken by the wind,
so visible forms, tastes, sounds, smells and touches, all of them,
"and things desirable and undesirable, do not stir one who is steady;
the mind stands firm and set free, and they observe its passing away" [Mahāva. 244; A. Ni. 6.55]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "there is adding to what has been done." ^5-266

Should it not be said that "a worthy one falls away from arahantship"? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, these five things lead to the falling away of a temporarily liberated monk. Which five? Delight in activity, delight in talk, delight in sleep, delight in company, and not reviewing the mind according to how it has been liberated. These, monks, are the five things that lead to the falling away of a temporarily liberated monk" [A. Ni. 5.149]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case, a worthy one falls away from arahantship.
Does a worthy one have delight in activity? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one have delight in activity? Yes. Does a worthy one have greed, sensual greed, obsession by sensual greed, the fetter of sensual greed, the flood of sensuality, the bond of sensuality, the hindrance of sensual desire? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one have delight in talk, does a worthy one have delight in sleep, does a worthy one have delight in company? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one have delight in company? Yes. Does a worthy one have greed, sensual greed, obsession by sensual greed, the fetter of sensual greed, the flood of sensuality, the bond of sensuality, the hindrance of sensual desire? That should not be said. ^5-267

Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. When a worthy one falls away from arahantship, obsessed by what do they fall away? They fall away obsessed by greed. Dependent on what does the obsession arise? It arises dependent on an underlying tendency. Does a worthy one have underlying tendencies? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one have underlying tendencies? Yes. Does a worthy one have the underlying tendency to sensual greed, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to greed for existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance? That should not be said.
They fall away obsessed by hatred… they fall away obsessed by delusion… Dependent on what does the obsession arise? It arises dependent on an underlying tendency. Does a worthy one have underlying tendencies? That should not be said…
Does a worthy one have underlying tendencies? Yes. Does a worthy one have the underlying tendency to sensual greed… the underlying tendency to ignorance? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. When a worthy one falls away from arahantship, what increases in them? Greed increases. Does identity view increase, does doubt increase, does clinging to rules and rituals increase? That should not be said. Hatred increases… delusion increases — does identity view increase, does doubt increase, does clinging to rules and rituals increase? That should not be said.
Does a worthy one fall away from arahantship? Yes. Does a worthy one build up? That should not be said. Does a worthy one tear down? That should not be said. Does a worthy one abandon? That should not be said. Does a worthy one cling? That should not be said. Does a worthy one scatter? That should not be said. Does a worthy one bind together? That should not be said. Does a worthy one put out? That should not be said. Does a worthy one kindle? That should not be said.
But doesn't a worthy one neither build up nor tear down, but stand having torn down? Yes. If a worthy one neither builds up nor tears down, but stands having torn down, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
But doesn't a worthy one neither abandon nor cling, but stand having abandoned? Yes. If a worthy one neither abandons nor clings, but stands having abandoned, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
But doesn't a worthy one neither scatter nor bind together, but stand having scattered? Yes. If a worthy one neither scatters nor binds together, but stands having scattered, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
But doesn't a worthy one neither put out nor kindle, but stand having put out? Yes. If a worthy one neither puts out nor kindles, but stands having put out, then surely you must not say: "A worthy one falls away from arahantship."
The Discussion of Falling Away is finished. ^5-268

### Discussion of the Holy Life ^5-3-0

#### Plain Discussion of the Holy Life ^5-3-1-0

Is there no living of the holy life (the life of spiritual training) among the gods? Yes. Are all gods dull, deaf and dumb [variant: eḷamūgā (Syā.)], unintelligent, communicating by hand signs, unable to understand the meaning of what is well spoken and badly spoken; are all gods without confidence in the Buddha, without confidence in the Dhamma, without confidence in the Community; do they not attend on the Buddha, the Blessed One, not ask the Buddha, the Blessed One, questions, and are they not pleased when the Buddha, the Blessed One, has answered a question; are all gods burdened with the obstruction of action, burdened with the obstruction of defilements, burdened with the obstruction of results, without faith, without wholesome desire, lacking wisdom, incapable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states; are all gods killers of their mother, killers of their father, killers of worthy ones (arahants), shedders of a Buddha's blood, splitters of the Community; are all gods ones who kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, speak divisively, speak harshly, engage in idle chatter, are covetous, have minds full of ill will, and hold wrong view? That should not be said…
But aren't there gods who are not dull, not deaf and dumb, intelligent, not communicating by hand signs, able to understand the meaning of what is well spoken and badly spoken; aren't there gods who have confidence in the Buddha, confidence in the Dhamma, confidence in the Community, who attend on the Buddha, the Blessed One, ask the Buddha, the Blessed One, questions, and are pleased when the Buddha, the Blessed One, has answered a question; aren't there gods who are not burdened with the obstruction of action, not burdened with the obstruction of defilements, not burdened with the obstruction of results, who have faith, have wholesome desire, are wise, capable of entering the fixed course of rightness in wholesome states; aren't there gods who are not killers of their mother, not killers of their father, not killers of worthy ones, not shedders of a Buddha's blood, not splitters of the Community; aren't there gods who do not kill living beings, do not take what is not given, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, do not speak divisively, do not speak harshly, do not engage in idle chatter, are not covetous, have minds free of ill will, and hold right view? Yes.
If there are gods who are not dull, not deaf and dumb, intelligent, not communicating by hand signs, able to understand the meaning of what is well spoken and badly spoken… there are gods who have confidence in the Buddha… who hold right view, then surely you must not say: "There is no living of the holy life among the gods." ^5-269

Is there living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Is there going forth there, shaving of the head, wearing of the ochre robe, carrying of the alms bowl; do Fully Awakened Buddhas arise among the gods, do solitary Buddhas arise, does a pair of chief disciples arise? That should not be said…
Since there is no going forth among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where there is going forth, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no going forth, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where there is going forth, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no going forth, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. Is it only for one who goes forth that there is living of the holy life, and for one who does not go forth that there is none? That should not be said…
Since there is no shaving of the head among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where there is shaving of the head, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no shaving of the head, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where there is shaving of the head, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no shaving of the head, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. Is it only for one whose head is shaven that there is living of the holy life, and for one whose head is not shaven that there is none? That should not be said…
Since there is no wearing of the ochre robe among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where there is wearing of the ochre robe, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no wearing of the ochre robe, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where there is wearing of the ochre robe, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no wearing of the ochre robe, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. Is it only for one who wears the ochre robe that there is living of the holy life, and for one who does not wear the ochre robe that there is none? That should not be said…
Since there is no carrying of the alms bowl among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where there is carrying of the alms bowl, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no carrying of the alms bowl, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where there is carrying of the alms bowl, is there living of the holy life only there, and where there is no carrying of the alms bowl, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. Is it only for one who carries the alms bowl that there is living of the holy life, and for one who does not carry the alms bowl that there is none? That should not be said…
Since Fully Awakened Buddhas do not arise among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where Fully Awakened Buddhas arise, is there living of the holy life only there, and where Fully Awakened Buddhas do not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where Fully Awakened Buddhas arise, is there living of the holy life only there, and where Fully Awakened Buddhas do not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. The Blessed One was born at Lumbinī, became fully awakened at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and set the wheel of the Dhamma in motion at Bārāṇasī; is there living of the holy life only there, and none anywhere else? That should not be said…
Since solitary Buddhas do not arise among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where solitary Buddhas arise, is there living of the holy life only there, and where solitary Buddhas do not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where solitary Buddhas arise, is there living of the holy life only there, and where solitary Buddhas do not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. Solitary Buddhas arise in the central regions; is there living of the holy life only there, and none anywhere else? That should not be said…
Since a pair of chief disciples does not arise among the gods, is there no living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Where a pair of chief disciples arises, is there living of the holy life only there, and where a pair of chief disciples does not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? That should not be said… Where a pair of chief disciples arises, is there living of the holy life only there, and where a pair of chief disciples does not arise, is there no living of the holy life there? Yes. The pair of chief disciples arose in Magadha; is there living of the holy life only there, and none anywhere else? That should not be said… ^5-270

Is there living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Is there living of the holy life among all gods? That should not be said…
Is there living of the holy life among human beings? Yes. Is there living of the holy life among all human beings? That should not be said…
Is there living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. Is there living of the holy life among the gods who are beings without perception? That should not be said…
Is there living of the holy life among human beings? Yes. Is there living of the holy life in the border regions, among the foreigners [variant: milakkhūsu (Syā., Ka.)] who do not understand, where there is no going of monks, nuns, male lay followers and female lay followers? That should not be said.
Is there living of the holy life among the gods? In some places there is, in some places there is not. Among the gods who are beings without perception, is it the case that in some places there is living of the holy life and in some places there is not; among the gods who are beings with perception [variant: asaññasattesu (Ka.)], is it the case that in some places there is and in some places there is not? That should not be said.
Among the gods, is it the case that in some places there is living of the holy life and in some places there is not? Yes. Where is there, and where is there not? Among the gods who are beings without perception there is no living of the holy life; among the gods who are beings with perception [variant: asaññasattesu (Ka.)] there is living of the holy life. Among the gods who are beings without perception, is there no living of the holy life? Yes. Among the gods who are beings with perception [variant: asaññasattesu (Ka.)], is there no living of the holy life? That should not be said.
Among the gods who are beings with perception, is there living of the holy life? Yes. Among the gods who are beings without perception, is there living of the holy life? That should not be said.
Is there living of the holy life among human beings? In some places there is, in some places there is not. In the border regions, among the foreigners who do not understand, where there is no going of monks, nuns, male lay followers and female lay followers, is it the case that in some places there is living of the holy life and in some places there is not; in the central regions, is it the case that in some places there is and in some places there is not? That should not be said.
Among human beings, is it the case that in some places there is living of the holy life and in some places there is not? Yes. Where is there, and where is there not? In the border regions, among the foreigners who do not understand, where there is no going of monks, nuns, male lay followers and female lay followers, there is no living of the holy life; in the central regions there is living of the holy life. In the border regions, among the foreigners who do not understand, where there is no going of monks, nuns, male lay followers and female lay followers, is there no living of the holy life? Yes. In the central regions, is there no living of the holy life? That should not be said.
In the central regions, is there living of the holy life? Yes. Is there living of the holy life in the border regions, among the foreigners who do not understand, where there is no going of monks, nuns, male lay followers and female lay followers? That should not be said.
Is there living of the holy life among the gods? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, in three respects the human beings of Jambudīpa surpass both the human beings of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Thirty-three. Which three? They are brave, they are mindful, and here there is the living of the holy life" [A. Ni. 9.21]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case, there is no living of the holy life among the gods.
Did the Blessed One say at Sāvatthī: "Here there is the living of the holy life"? Yes. Is there living of the holy life only at Sāvatthī, and none anywhere else? That should not be said. ^5-271

For a person who is a non-returner, the five lower fetters have been abandoned and the five higher fetters have not been abandoned; when they have passed away from here and been reborn there, where does the fruit arise for them? There. If for a person who is a non-returner the five lower fetters have been abandoned and the five higher fetters have not been abandoned, and when they have passed away from here and been reborn there the fruit arises for them there, then surely you must not say: "There is no living of the holy life among the gods."
For a person who is a non-returner, the five lower fetters have been abandoned and the five higher fetters have not been abandoned; when they have passed away from here and been reborn there, where is the laying down of the burden, where the full understanding of suffering, where the abandoning of defilements, where the realization of cessation, where the penetration of the unshakeable? There. If for a person who is a non-returner the five lower fetters have been abandoned and the five higher fetters have not been abandoned, and when they have passed away from here and been reborn there the penetration of the unshakeable is there, then surely you must not say: "There is no living of the holy life among the gods."
For a person who is a non-returner, the five lower fetters have been abandoned and the five higher fetters have not been abandoned; when they have passed away from here and been reborn there, the fruit arises there, the laying down of the burden is there, the full understanding of suffering is there, the abandoning of defilements is there, the realization of cessation is there, the penetration of the unshakeable is there; in what sense, then, do you say: "There is no living of the holy life among the gods"? Well, the non-returner person realizes the fruit there by means of the path developed here [variant: sacchikaroti (many editions)]. ^5-272

#### Discussion of the Holy Life by Comparison ^5-3-2-0

Does a non-returner person realize the fruit there by means of the path developed here? Yes. Does a stream-enterer person realize the fruit here by means of the path developed there? That should not be said.
Does a non-returner person realize the fruit there by means of the path developed here? Yes. Does a once-returner person, a person who attains final nibbāna (final release) here [variant: idhaparinibbāyī (?)], realize the fruit here by means of the path developed there? That should not be said.
Does a stream-enterer person realize the fruit here by means of the path developed here? Yes. Does a non-returner person realize the fruit there by means of the path developed there? That should not be said.
Does a once-returner person, a person who attains final nibbāna here, realize the fruit here by means of the path developed here? Yes. Does a non-returner person realize the fruit there by means of the path developed there? That should not be said…
For a person who reaches completion after leaving here, is the path developed and yet the defilements are not abandoned? Yes. For a person practising for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, is the path developed and yet the defilements are not abandoned? That should not be said…
For a person who reaches completion after leaving here, is the path developed and yet the defilements are not abandoned? Yes. For a person practising for the realization of the fruit of once-returning… for a person practising for the realization of arahantship, is the path developed and yet the defilements are not abandoned? That should not be said…
For a person practising for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, are the path developed and the defilements abandoned at one and the same time, neither before nor after? Yes. For a person who reaches completion after leaving here, are the path developed and the defilements abandoned at one and the same time, neither before nor after? That should not be said.
For a person practising for the realization of the fruit of once-returning… for a person practising for the realization of arahantship, are the path developed and the defilements abandoned at one and the same time, neither before nor after? Yes. For a person who reaches completion after leaving here, are the path developed and the defilements abandoned at one and the same time, neither before nor after? That should not be said.
Is a non-returner person, who has done what had to be done and whose development is complete, reborn there? Yes. Is a worthy one reborn? That should not be said.
Is a worthy one reborn? Yes. Is there renewed existence for a worthy one? That should not be said.
Is there renewed existence for a worthy one? Yes. Does a worthy one go from existence to existence, from destination to destination, from one round of rebirth to another, from rebirth to rebirth? That should not be said.
Is a non-returner person, who has done what had to be done, whose development is complete, but who has not laid down the burden, reborn there? Yes. Do they develop the path again in order to lay down the burden? That should not be said.
Is a non-returner person, who has done what had to be done, whose development is complete, but who has not fully understood suffering, not abandoned the defilements, not realized cessation, not penetrated the unshakeable, reborn there? Yes. Do they develop the path again in order to penetrate the unshakeable? That should not be said.
Is a non-returner person, who has done what had to be done, whose development is complete, but who has not laid down the burden, reborn there, and do they not develop the path again in order to lay down the burden? Yes. Do they then attain final nibbāna there without having laid down the burden? That should not be said.
Is a non-returner person, who has done what had to be done, whose development is complete, but who has not fully understood suffering, not abandoned the defilements, not realized cessation, not penetrated the unshakeable, reborn there, and do they not develop the path again in order to penetrate the unshakeable? Yes. Do they then attain final nibbāna there without having penetrated the unshakeable? That should not be said. Just as a deer struck by an arrow dies even after going a long way, so too the non-returner person realizes the fruit there by means of the path developed here.
Just as a deer struck by an arrow, even after going a long way, dies with the arrow still in it, so too does the non-returner person, by means of the path developed here, attain final nibbāna there with the arrow still in them? That should not be said…
The Discussion of the Holy Life is finished. ^5-273

Then are they partly a worthy one and partly not a worthy one; are they partly one who has attained, obtained, reached and realized arahantship [variant: arahattaṃ patto (?)] and who dwells having entered upon it and dwells having touched it with the body, and partly one who does not dwell having touched it with the body; are they partly free from greed, free from hatred, free from delusion, one who has done what had to be done, who has laid down the load, who has reached their own goal, whose fetters of existence are utterly destroyed, who is completely liberated through final knowledge, who has lifted the cross-bar, filled in the moat, pulled out the pillar, who has no bolt, a noble one, whose banner is lowered, whose burden is put down, who is unfettered, who has won complete victory; one by whom suffering has been fully understood, its origin abandoned, its cessation realized, the path developed; by whom what is to be directly known has been directly known, what is to be fully understood has been fully understood, what is to be abandoned has been abandoned, what is to be developed has been developed, what is to be realized has been realized, (partly what is to be realized has been realized,) [( ) (?)] and partly what is to be realized has not been realized? Should it not be said that "one abandons the defilements part by part"? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"Gradually, little by little, moment by moment, the wise one
should blow away their own impurities, as a smith does with silver" [Dha. Pa. 239, in the Dhammapada]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "one abandons the defilements part by part."
Does one abandon the defilements part by part? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"Together with their attainment of vision,
three things are abandoned:
identity view and doubt,
and whatever there may be of rules and rituals.
They are freed from the four lower realms,
and incapable [variant: abhabbo (Sī., Syā.)] of doing the six grave wrongs" [Khu. Pā. 6.10; Su. Ni. 233]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "one abandons the defilements part by part."
Does one abandon the defilements part by part? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, at the time when the dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma arises in a noble disciple — ‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’ — then, monks, together with the arising of vision, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals" [in the Aṅguttara Nikāya]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "one abandons the defilements part by part."

### Discussion of Abandoning ^5-4-0

#### Discussion without Citing the Discourses ^5-4-1-0

Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will? Yes. Do they abandon them absolutely, abandon them without remainder, abandon them so that they never return, abandon them together with the root, abandon them together with craving, abandon them together with the underlying tendency, abandon them by noble knowledge, abandon them by the noble path, abandon them while penetrating the unshakeable, abandon them while realizing the fruit of non-returning? That should not be said…
Does an ordinary person suppress sensual desire and ill will? Yes. Do they suppress them absolutely, suppress them without remainder, suppress them so that they never return, suppress them together with the root, suppress them together with craving, suppress them together with the underlying tendency, suppress them by noble knowledge, suppress them by the noble path, suppress them while penetrating the unshakeable, suppress them while realizing the fruit of non-returning? That should not be said…
Does a person practising for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual desire and ill will, and do they abandon them absolutely, abandon them without remainder… abandon them while realizing the fruit of non-returning? Yes. Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will, and do they abandon them absolutely, abandon them without remainder… abandon them while realizing the fruit of non-returning? That should not be said…

That should not be said…
Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will? Yes. By which path? By a path belonging to the realm of form. Is a path belonging to the realm of form one that leads out, leads to destruction, leads to awakening, leads to dismantling, is free of taints, not subject to the fetters, not subject to the knots, not subject to the floods, not subject to the bonds, not subject to the hindrances, not seized upon, not subject to clinging, not subject to defilement? That should not be said. But isn't a path belonging to the realm of form one that does not lead out, does not lead to destruction, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to dismantling, is accompanied by taints, subject to the fetters… subject to defilement? Yes. If a path belonging to the realm of form is one that does not lead out, does not lead to destruction… is subject to defilement, then surely you must not say: "An ordinary person abandons sensual desire and ill will by a path belonging to the realm of form."
Does a person practising for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual desire and ill will by the path of non-returning, and is that path one that leads out, leads to destruction, leads to awakening, leads to dismantling, is free of taints… not subject to defilement? Yes. Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will by a path belonging to the realm of form, and is that path one that leads out, leads to destruction, leads to awakening, leads to dismantling, is free of taints… not subject to defilement? That should not be said…
Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will by a path belonging to the realm of form, and is that path one that does not lead out, does not lead to destruction, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to dismantling, is accompanied by taints… subject to defilement? Yes. Does a person practising for the realization of the fruit of non-returning abandon sensual desire and ill will by the path of non-returning, and is that path one that does not lead out, does not lead to destruction, does not lead to awakening, does not lead to dismantling, is accompanied by taints… subject to defilement? That should not be said… ^5-279

Does an ordinary person who is free from greed for sensual pleasures become established in the fruit of non-returning upon breaking through to the Dhamma? Yes. Do they become established in arahantship (the state of a worthy one)? That should not be said…
Does an ordinary person who is free from greed for sensual pleasures become established in the fruit of non-returning upon breaking through to the Dhamma? Yes. Do they develop three paths at one and the same time, neither before nor after? That should not be said…
Do they develop three paths at one and the same time, neither before nor after? Yes. Do they realize three fruits of the ascetic life at one and the same time, neither before nor after? That should not be said…
Do they realize three fruits of the ascetic life at one and the same time, neither before nor after? Yes. Is there a coming together of three contacts, three feelings, three perceptions, three intentions, three states of mind, three kinds of faith, three kinds of energy, three kinds of mindfulness, three kinds of concentration, three kinds of wisdom? That should not be said…
Does an ordinary person who is free from greed for sensual pleasures become established in the fruit of non-returning upon breaking through to the Dhamma? Yes. By the path of stream-entry? That should not be said…
By the path of once-returning? That should not be said. By which path, then? By the path of non-returning. Do they abandon identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals by the path of non-returning? That should not be said… ^5-280

#### Discussion Citing the Discourses ^5-4-2-0

Do they abandon identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals by the path of non-returning? Yes. But didn't the Blessed One declare that the fruit of stream-entry comes from abandoning three fetters? Yes. If the Blessed One declared that the fruit of stream-entry comes from abandoning three fetters, then surely you must not say: "One abandons identity view, doubt and clinging to rules and rituals by the path of non-returning." Do they abandon gross sensual desire and gross ill will by the path of non-returning? That should not be said…
Do they abandon gross sensual desire and gross ill will by the path of non-returning? Yes. But didn't the Blessed One declare that the fruit of once-returning comes from the weakening of sensual desire and ill will? Yes. If the Blessed One declared that the fruit of once-returning comes from the weakening of sensual desire and ill will, then surely you must not say: "One abandons gross sensual desire and gross ill will by the path of non-returning."
Does an ordinary person who is free from greed for sensual pleasures become established in the fruit of non-returning upon breaking through to the Dhamma? Yes. Do all who break through to the Dhamma become established in the fruit of non-returning upon breaking through to the Dhamma? That should not be said…
Should it not be said that "an ordinary person abandons sensual desire and ill will"? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"In times past there were [variant: ahiṃsakā (A. Ni. 6.54)] six teachers of great renown,
free of the stench of corruption, intent on compassion [variant: karuṇādhimuttā (Sī., Ka.)], gone beyond the fetter of sensual desire.
"Having made sensual desire fade away, they went to the Brahmā world;
and their disciples, too, were many hundreds.
"Free of the stench of corruption, intent on compassion, gone beyond the fetter of sensual desire,
having made sensual desire fade away, they went to the Brahmā world" [A. Ni. 6.54]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case, an ordinary person abandons sensual desire and ill will.
Does an ordinary person abandon sensual desire and ill will? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, that teacher Sunetta, though he lived so long and endured so long, was not freed from birth, ageing and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, griefs and despairs; he was not freed from suffering, I say. Why is that? Because he did not understand and did not penetrate four things. Which four? Because he did not understand and did not penetrate noble virtue, noble concentration, noble wisdom and noble liberation. But now, monks, noble virtue has been understood and penetrated, noble concentration has been understood and penetrated, noble wisdom has been understood and penetrated, noble liberation has been understood and penetrated; craving for existence has been cut off, what leads to existence is destroyed, and now there is no renewed existence.
"Virtue, concentration and wisdom, and unsurpassed liberation —
these things have been understood by Gotama, the renowned.
"So the Buddha, having directly known them, taught the Dhamma to the monks:
the teacher, the maker of an end of suffering, the one with vision, has attained final nibbāna (final release)" [A. Ni. 7.66]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "an ordinary person abandons sensual desire and ill will."
The Discussion of Abandoning is finished. ^5-281

### Discussion of "Everything Exists" ^5-5-0

#### Reasoning about the Thesis ^5-5-1-0

Does everything exist? Yes. Does everything exist everywhere? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. Does everything exist at all times? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. Does everything exist in every way? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. Does everything exist in everything? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. Does everything exist, taking it as not joined together? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. Does even what does not exist exist? That should not be said. Does everything exist? Yes. The view that "everything exists" — does that view exist as wrong view, and does that same view exist as right view, in this way? That should not be said. (Abbreviated.) Reasoning about the thesis. ^5-282

#### Comparison of Times ^5-5-2-0

Does the past exist? Yes. But isn't the past ceased, gone, changed, vanished, completely vanished? Yes. If the past is ceased, gone, changed, vanished, completely vanished, then surely you must not say: "The past exists."
Does the future exist? Yes. But isn't the future unborn, not come to be, not arisen, not produced, not fully produced, not manifested? Yes. If the future is unborn, not come to be, not arisen, not produced, not fully produced, not manifested, then surely you must not say: "The future exists."
Does the present exist, and is the present not ceased, not gone, not changed, not vanished, not completely vanished? Yes. #### Discussion Clarifying the Words ^5-5-9-0

Does the past exist? Yes. Is what exists the past? Of what exists, some may be past and some may be not past.
Acknowledge the refutation. If the past exists, and of what exists some may be past and some may be not past, then the past is not past, and what is not past is past. What you say here — that it should be said that "the past exists; of what exists, some may be past and some may be not past; so the past is not past, and what is not past is past" — is wrong.
But if it is not the case that the past is not past and what is not past is past, then surely you must not say: "The past exists; of what exists, some may be past and some may be not past." What you say here — that it should be said that "the past exists; of what exists, some may be past and some may be not past; so the past is not past, and what is not past is past" — is wrong.
Does the future exist? Yes. Is what exists the future? Of what exists, some may be future and some may be not future.
Acknowledge the refutation. If the future exists, and of what exists some may be future and some may be not future, then the future is not future, and what is not future is future. What you say here — that it should be said that "the future exists; of what exists, some may be future and some may be not future; so the future is not future, and what is not future is future" — is wrong.
But if it is not the case that the future is not future and what is not future is future, then surely you must not say: "The future exists; of what exists, some may be future and some may be not future." What you say here — that it should be said that "the future exists; of what exists, some may be future and some may be not future; so the future is not future, and what is not future is future" — is wrong.
Does the present exist? Yes. Is what exists the present? Of what exists, some may be present and some may be not present.
Acknowledge the refutation. If the present exists, and of what exists some may be present and some may be not present, then the present is not present, and what is not present is present. What you say here — that it should be said that "the present exists; of what exists, some may be present and some may be not present; so the present is not present, and what is not present is present" — is wrong.
But if it is not the case that the present is not present and what is not present is present, then surely you must not say: "The present exists; of what exists, some may be present and some may be not present." What you say here — that it should be said that "the present exists; of what exists, some may be present and some may be not present; so the present is not present, and what is not present is present" — is wrong.
Does nibbāna exist? Yes. Is what exists nibbāna? Of what exists, some may be nibbāna and some may be not nibbāna.
Acknowledge the refutation. If nibbāna exists, and of what exists some may be nibbāna and some may be not nibbāna, then nibbāna is not nibbāna, and what is not nibbāna is nibbāna. What you say here — that it should be said that "nibbāna exists; of what exists, some may be nibbāna and some may be not nibbāna; so nibbāna is not nibbāna, and what is not nibbāna is nibbāna" — is wrong.
But if it is not the case that nibbāna is not nibbāna and what is not nibbāna is nibbāna, then surely you must not say: "Nibbāna exists; of what exists, some may be nibbāna and some may be not nibbāna." What you say here — that it should be said that "nibbāna exists; of what exists, some may be nibbāna and some may be not nibbāna; so nibbāna is not nibbāna, and what is not nibbāna is nibbāna" — is wrong. ^5-295

#### Proof from the Discourses ^5-5-10-0

Should it not be said that "the past exists, the future exists"? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, whatever material form there is, whether past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — this is called the aggregate of material form. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever mental formations… whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near — this is called the aggregate of consciousness" [S. Ni. 3.48]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case, the past exists and the future exists.
Does the past exist, and does the future exist? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, there are these three pathways of language, pathways of naming, pathways of designation, which are unmixed, have never been mixed, are not being mixed and will not be mixed, and which are not rejected by wise ascetics and brahmins. Which three? Monks, the material form that is past, ceased, gone, changed — its reckoning is ‘it was’, its name is ‘it was’, its designation is ‘it was’; its reckoning is not ‘it is’, its reckoning is not ‘it will be’. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever mental formations… whatever consciousness is past, ceased, gone, changed — its reckoning is ‘it was’, its name is ‘it was’, its designation is ‘it was’; its reckoning is not ‘it is’, its reckoning is not ‘it will be’.
"Monks, the material form that is unborn, not manifested — its reckoning is ‘it will be’, its name is ‘it will be’, its designation is ‘it will be’; its reckoning is not ‘it is’, its reckoning is not ‘it was’. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever mental formations… whatever consciousness is unborn, not manifested — its reckoning is ‘it will be’, its name is ‘it will be’, its designation is ‘it will be’; its reckoning is not ‘it is’, its reckoning is not ‘it was’.
"Monks, the material form that is born, manifested — its reckoning is ‘it is’, its name is ‘it is’, its designation is ‘it is’; its reckoning is not ‘it was’, its reckoning is not ‘it will be’. Whatever feeling… whatever perception… whatever mental formations… whatever consciousness is born, manifested — its reckoning is ‘it is’, its name is ‘it is’, its designation is ‘it is’; its reckoning is not ‘it was’, its reckoning is not ‘it will be’. These, monks, are the three pathways of language, pathways of naming, pathways of designation, which are unmixed, have never been mixed, are not being mixed and will not be mixed, and which are not rejected by wise ascetics and brahmins.
"Monks, even the people of Ukkalā, Vassa and Bhañña, who taught that there is no cause, taught that action has no effect, and taught that nothing exists, did not think that these three pathways of language, pathways of naming, pathways of designation should be criticized or rejected. Why is that? For fear of blame, opposition and censure" [in the Saṃyutta Nikāya]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "the past exists, the future exists."
Does the past exist? Yes. But didn't the venerable Phagguna say this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, is there that eye by which one, in describing the past Buddhas — who have attained final nibbāna, who have cut off proliferation, cut off the road, ended the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering — could describe them? Venerable sir, is there that tongue… venerable sir, is there that mind by which one, in describing the past Buddhas — who have attained final nibbāna, who have cut off proliferation, cut off the road, ended the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering — could describe them?"
"There is no such eye, Phagguna, by which one, in describing the past Buddhas — who have attained final nibbāna, who have cut off proliferation, cut off the road, ended the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering — could describe them. There is no such tongue, Phagguna… there is no such mind, Phagguna, by which one, in describing the past Buddhas — who have attained final nibbāna, who have cut off proliferation, cut off the road, ended the cycle, and passed beyond all suffering — could describe them" [S. Ni. 4.83]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "the past exists."

But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, if there is greed for the nutriment of edible food, if there is delight, if there is craving, then consciousness becomes established there and grows. Where there is growth of mental formations, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future, there is birth, ageing and death in the future. Where there is birth, ageing and death in the future, that, monks, I say, is accompanied by sorrow, by dust [variant: sadaraṃ (S. Ni. 2.64); that reading is more fitting] and by despair.
"Monks, if for the nutriment of contact… for the nutriment of mental intention… for the nutriment of consciousness there is greed, if there is delight… is accompanied by dust and by despair, I say" [S. Ni. 2.64]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case, the future exists.
Does the future exist? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, if there is no greed for the nutriment of edible food, if there is no delight, if there is no craving, then consciousness does not become established there and does not grow. Where there is no growth of mental formations, there is no production of renewed existence in the future. Where there is no production of renewed existence in the future, there is no birth, ageing and death in the future. Where there is no birth, ageing and death in the future, that, monks, I say, is without sorrow, without dust and without despair.
"Monks, if for the nutriment of contact… for the nutriment of mental intention… for the nutriment of consciousness there is no greed, if there is no delight… is without dust and without despair, I say" [S. Ni. 2.64]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "the future exists."

That should not be said… In that case, material form in a way exists and in a way does not exist; feeling… perception… mental formations… consciousness in a way exists and in a way does not exist.
The Discussion of "In a Way It Exists" is finished.
Here is its summary:
Being found, falling away, the living of the holy life, part by part;
full understanding, the abandoning of sensual desire, the doctrine that everything exists, the sense base;
the past and future in part [variant: atītānāgatesu bhāgo (Syā.)], all things are foundations of mindfulness;
"In a way it exists, in a way it does not exist."
The First Chapter,
The Great Chapter. ^5-306

Does a worthy one have lack of knowledge? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows [variant: jānatāhaṃ (Sī.), jānatvāhaṃ (Syā., Pī., Ka.)] and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And knowing what, monks, seeing what, does the destruction of the taints come about? ‘Such is material form, such is the origin of material form, such is the passing away of material form; such is feeling… such is perception… such are mental formations… such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness’ — it is for one who knows thus, monks, who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints comes about" [S. Ni. 3.101; Itivu. 102; S. Ni. 5.1095]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has lack of knowledge."
Does a worthy one have lack of knowledge? Yes. It is for one who knows thus, monks, who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints comes about" [S. Ni. 5.1095]? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. #### (12) 3. Discussion of Uncertainty ^5-10-4-0

Does a worthy one (arahant) have uncertainty? Yes. Does a worthy one have doubt, obsession by doubt, the fetter of doubt, the hindrance of doubt? That should not be said…

Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And knowing what, monks, seeing what, does the destruction of the taints come about? ‘Such is material form’… ‘such is the passing away of consciousness’ — it is for one who knows thus, monks, who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints comes about"? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And knowing what, monks, seeing what, does the destruction of the taints come about? ‘This is suffering,’ monks… ‘This is the way of practice leading to the cessation of suffering’ — for one who knows and sees this, the destruction of the taints comes about. It is for one who knows thus, monks, who sees thus, that the destruction of the taints comes about"? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, without directly knowing the all, without fully understanding it, without making it fade away and without abandoning it, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering; but, monks, by directly knowing the all, fully understanding it, making it fade away and abandoning it, one is capable of the destruction of suffering"? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Together with their attainment of vision… and incapable of doing the six grave wrongs"? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say: "Monks, at the time when the dust-free, stainless eye of the Dhamma arises in a noble disciple — ‘Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’ — then, monks, together with the arising of vision, three fetters are abandoned in the noble disciple: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and rituals"? Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. But did the Blessed One not say:
"When things become manifest
to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all their uncertainties vanish,
since they understand things together with their cause.
"When things become manifest
to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
then all their uncertainties vanish,
since they have come to know the destruction of conditions.
"When things become manifest
to the ardent, meditating brahmin,
they stand dispelling the army of Māra,
like the sun [variant: suriyova (Sī., Syā., Kaṃ., Pī.)] lighting up the sky [Mahāva. 3; Udā. 3].
"Whatever uncertainties there are, about here or beyond,
whether known to oneself or known through others,
meditators [variant: ye jhāyino (in the Udāna)] abandon them all,
the ardent ones living the holy life (the life of spiritual training) [Udā. 47, also in the Udāna].
"Those who have gone beyond uncertainty among beings full of uncertainty,
free from hesitation and unfettered — what is given to them bears great fruit.
"Such is the proclaiming of the Dhamma here;
no disciple is uncertain about anything in it.
The one who has crossed the flood [variant: nitiṇṇaoghaṃ (Sī., Ka.), nittiṇṇaoghaṃ (Syā., Kaṃ.)] and cut off doubt,
the Buddha, the Conqueror, lord of people, we revere" [D. Ni. 2.354]?
Is there really such a discourse? Yes. In that case it should not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty."
Should it not be said that "a worthy one has uncertainty"? Yes. But isn't it the case that a worthy one might be uncertain about the names and clans of women and men, might be uncertain about the right road and the wrong road, might be uncertain about the names of grasses, wood and trees? Yes. If a worthy one might be uncertain about the names and clans of women and men, might be uncertain about the right road and the wrong road, might be uncertain about the names of grasses, wood and trees, then surely you must also say: "A worthy one has uncertainty."
Since a worthy one might be uncertain about the names and clans of women and men, might be uncertain about the right road and the wrong road, might be uncertain about the names of grasses, wood and trees, does a worthy one have uncertainty? Yes. Might a worthy one be uncertain about the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning, or arahantship (the state of a worthy one)? That should not be said…
The Discussion of Uncertainty is finished. ^5-321

Does one who is in a meditative attainment have verbal expression? Yes. Do those in a meditative attainment have verbal expression everywhere? That should not be said…
